title: Undo/Redo Stack
description: Command-pattern undo/redo — each action is an object with apply/revert. Two stacks: done and undone. Doing a fresh command clears the redo stack.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the API and the timeline semantics.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I need a History class with three methods — `do(cmd)` runs a command, `undo()` reverses the most recent one, and `redo()` re-runs the most recently undone one. Each command is some object that knows how to apply itself and how to revert itself."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• What shape are commands — `{apply, revert}` callable objects, or just plain data I have to interpret? (I'll assume callable for now.)
• If the user does an action, undoes it, then does a NEW action — does the redo of the original still work, or is it gone? (This is the load-bearing semantic question.)
• Should `undo` on an empty history throw, or silently no-op? (UI-wise, no-op is friendlier — disabled buttons just don't fire.)
• Any depth limit on the history, or unbounded?
sections.why: The 'new action after undo clears redo' question is the entire interview. Every editor on earth works this way — VSCode, Photoshop, Google Docs — but candidates routinely miss it and ship a History where redo silently replays a stale command after the timeline has branched. Asking the question signals you've used an editor with an undo bug and remember the moment you noticed. The callable-vs-data clarification matters too: if commands are plain data, the History has to know how to invert them, which couples the two and ruins the Command pattern.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious single-stack design before discarding it.
sections.say: "The brute force is: one stack of applied commands. `do` pushes, `undo` pops and reverts. That handles undo cleanly. But where does redo go? I'd need a second structure — there's no way to recover an undone command from just the done stack once I've popped it. So I either keep a parallel 'undone' list, or I never actually pop on undo and instead track a cursor index into the stack. The cursor approach works but the index bookkeeping for 'fresh action truncates the future' is fiddly. Two stacks is cleaner: undo moves a command from done to undone, redo moves it back. The `do` method then explicitly clears undone — which makes the timeline-branching rule a single line of code instead of an off-by-one on a cursor."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the cursor variant out loud. (1) It's a real alternative — some implementations do use it — so dismissing it without explanation looks like ignorance. (2) The reason two-stacks wins is that the 'fresh do clears redo' rule becomes one explicit assignment (`this.undone = []`) instead of a slice on a cursor index, and explicitness is what makes the load-bearing rule survive future edits. Interviewers grade you on the tradeoff, not just the pick.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why two stacks, and what's the invariant that ties them together?
sections.say: "The data structure is two stacks: `done` and `undone`. The invariant is that they jointly represent a linear timeline — `done` is the past (commands applied, in order), `undone` is the future (commands waiting to be redone, top is next-to-redo). `do` pushes to done and clears undone, because performing a fresh action means we've branched off the old timeline and the future commands are no longer reachable. `undo` pops from done, reverts it, pushes to undone — that command moves from past to future. `redo` is the mirror — pops from undone, applies it, pushes to done. The 'new action after undo wipes redo' rule is the load-bearing one; without it, redo can replay a command that no longer makes sense against the current state."
sections.why: Naming the pattern (two-stacks-as-timeline) and the invariant (do-clears-undone) is the move. 'Use two stacks' alone is a guess; 'two stacks because they jointly model a timeline, and do clears undone because branching destroys the future' is a derivation. The interviewer's follow-up is almost always 'what happens if I do, undo, redo, do, redo?' — and the answer falls out of the invariant: the last redo is a no-op because the second `do` cleared the undone stack.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few operation sequences to confirm the model before writing the class.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through three sequences. Each shows the value of `x`, the done stack, and the undone stack after each op. The first is the canonical case — do, do, undo, do, undo, undo. The second covers the redo path. The third is the branching case — `do` after `undo` must clear the redo history."

examples.input: do(+1), do(+2), undo, do(+10), undo, undo
examples.note: Canonical case — third op `do(+10)` after the undo clears the undone stack, so the final undo can't redo the +2.
examples.trace:
init x=0, done=[], undone=[]
do(+1)   → x=1,  done=[+1],     undone=[]      results=[1]
do(+2)   → x=3,  done=[+1,+2],  undone=[]      results=[1,3]
undo     → pop +2, revert → x=1, done=[+1], undone=[+2]   results=[1,3,1]
do(+10)  → x=11, done=[+1,+10], undone=[]      ← cleared! +2 is gone   results=[1,3,1,11]
undo     → pop +10, revert → x=1, done=[+1], undone=[+10]  results=[1,3,1,11,1]
undo     → pop +1, revert → x=0, done=[], undone=[+10,+1]  results=[1,3,1,11,1,0]
return [1,3,1,11,1,0]

examples.note: Redo path works — after undo, redo replays the +5. The final undo on an empty done stack is a no-op (x stays at 0).
examples.trace:
init x=0, done=[], undone=[]
do(+5)   → x=5, done=[+5], undone=[]            results=[5]
undo     → pop +5, revert → x=0, done=[], undone=[+5]   results=[5,0]
redo     → pop +5, apply  → x=5, done=[+5], undone=[]   results=[5,0,5]
undo     → pop +5, revert → x=0, done=[], undone=[+5]   results=[5,0,5,0]
undo     → done empty — no-op, x unchanged              results=[5,0,5,0,0]
return [5,0,5,0,0]

examples.note: Branching case — `do(+7)` after the undo wipes undone, so the final `redo` is a no-op (the +4 is no longer reachable).
examples.trace:
init x=0, done=[], undone=[]
do(+3)   → x=3,  done=[+3],     undone=[]      results=[3]
do(+4)   → x=7,  done=[+3,+4],  undone=[]      results=[3,7]
undo     → pop +4, revert → x=3, done=[+3], undone=[+4]   results=[3,7,3]
do(+7)   → x=10, done=[+3,+7], undone=[]       ← cleared! +4 is gone   results=[3,7,3,10]
redo     → undone empty — no-op, x unchanged   results=[3,7,3,10,10]
return [3,7,3,10,10]

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the bug this problem is designed to catch — forgetting to clear undone in `do`. Without that line, the third example's final `redo` would replay the +4 against the new state (current x=10) and produce x=14, which is nonsense — the +4 was performed against a timeline where x was 3, not 10. The all-no-op trail in example 2 also shows why no-op-on-empty is the right call: the user pressed undo one extra time, and the value just stays where it is — silent, undramatic, no exception bubbling up to UI code.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Undo on empty done → no-op, return early. Don't throw — the UI just keeps the undo button disabled.
• Redo on empty undone → same, no-op.
• Do, undo, do → the second `do` must clear undone, otherwise a later redo replays a stale command against a branched timeline. This is the bug.
• Do, undo, undo (more undos than dos) → second undo no-ops cleanly because done is empty.
• Command throws inside apply/revert → the state machine is now corrupted (done stack thinks the command applied, but the side effect didn't). In production I'd wrap in try/catch and roll back; in an interview I'd flag it as something to discuss but not implement unless asked.
• Same command object pushed twice — fine, the stacks just hold references. Reverting twice would double-revert; that's the caller's problem to avoid.
• Unbounded growth — if the user does 100k actions, both stacks just grow. If memory mattered I'd cap done at N and drop the oldest, but undone has a natural bound (anything in undone came from done, and gets cleared on the next do)."
sections.why: The 'second do clears undone' bullet is the one to lean on — it's the bug that the trace exposed and the interviewer is probably checking for. The 'command throws' bullet is the senior-candidate flag: it shows you know real implementations have to deal with partial-apply failures, even if the in-interview scope is happy-path only. The unbounded-growth note shows you've thought about production scale without derailing into actually building an LRU.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity and place this pattern?
sections.say:
"Time is O(1) per operation — do/undo/redo are each one push, one pop, one apply or revert call, plus the constant-time clearing of undone in `do` (assigning a new empty array is O(1); freeing the old one is the GC's problem). No loops anywhere.

Space is O(n) where n is the number of applied commands — done plus undone together hold every command that's part of the current reachable timeline. Cleared commands become garbage and get collected.

The Command pattern (each command is `{apply, revert}`) is what generalizes this beyond a single 'number with +/-' demo. A text editor's commands might be `insertText` / `deleteText` pairs; a CAD program's might be `addShape` / `removeShape`. The History class doesn't change — only the commands do. That separation is the whole point of the pattern, and it's what lets the same History power VSCode's edit undo AND its workspace-layout undo without code reuse hacks.

If you wanted multi-user collaborative editing, this whole model breaks — concurrent edits don't form a stack, they form a graph, and you need operational transforms or CRDTs. Worth knowing the limit of the pattern."
sections.why: Naming the Command pattern explicitly is what elevates this from 'I can code an undo stack' to 'I know why this design exists'. The OT/CRDT mention at the end is the senior-engineer flourish — it shows you know when the pattern stops working, which is what a tech lead does. Interviewers love the inverse — candidates who can defend a pattern AND name where it breaks down.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of History operations on a number variable x. Each example is an op list — `do(+n)`, `undo`, or `redo`. The state panel shows the two stacks (done, undone) and the live value of x after each op. The trace collects x after every op into a `results` array so you can verify the timeline.

examples.label: do(+1), do(+2), undo, do(+10), undo, undo → x trail [1,3,1,11,1,0]
do(+5), undo, redo, undo, undo (no-op) → x trail [5,0,5,0,0]
do(+3), do(+4), undo, do(+7) clears redo, redo (no-op) → x trail [3,7,3,10,10]

trace: yield { line: 4, label: 'new History() — done=[], undone=[], x=0', state: { ops, x, done: [], undone: [], results: [] } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'op#' + k + ': do(+' + arg + ')', state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op, arg } };
yield { line: 8, label: 'cmd.apply() → x = ' + x, state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op, arg } };

yield { line: 9, label: 'done.push(+' + arg + ') → done=' + JSON.stringify(done.map(c => '+' + c.n)), state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op, arg } };

yield { line: 11, label: hadRedo ? 'fresh action — clear undone (branch destroys old future)' : 'undone already empty — nothing to clear', state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: [], results: [...results], op, arg } };
yield { line: 13, label: 'op#' + k + ': undo()', state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };
yield { line: 15, label: 'done is empty — no-op, return early', state: { ops, x, done: [], undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };
yield { line: 16, label: 'cmd.revert() → x = ' + x, state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };

yield { line: 17, label: 'undone.push(+' + cmd.n + ') → undone=' + JSON.stringify(undone.map(c => '+' + c.n)), state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };
yield { line: 19, label: 'op#' + k + ': redo()', state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };
yield { line: 21, label: 'undone is empty — no-op, return early', state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: [], results: [...results], op } };
yield { line: 22, label: 'cmd.apply() → x = ' + x, state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };

yield { line: 23, label: 'done.push(+' + cmd.n + ') → done=' + JSON.stringify(done.map(c => '+' + c.n)), state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], op } };

yield { line: 26, label: 'all ops processed — x trail = ' + JSON.stringify(results), state: { ops, x, done: done.map(c => '+' + c.n), undone: undone.map(c => '+' + c.n), results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Each command must be self-contained: apply() and revert() are inverses. The history doesn't know what the command does.
Doing a new action after an undo clears the undone stack — branching destroys the redo path. Standard editor behavior.
Undo and redo are no-ops on empty stacks. Don't throw — UI buttons just stay disabled.
Time O(1) per operation; Space O(n) where n is history depth.

alternates.label: Cursor-index into a single command array
alternates.when: Reach for this when you want to avoid two separate stacks and don't mind a slice on every do(). The cursor approach keeps all commands in one array and uses an index to mark the boundary between past and future. The two-stacks version is cleaner: 'clear undone' is one assignment vs 'slice to cursor'.
notes: `cursor` is the pivot: cmds[0..cursor-1] are applied (the 'done' stack); cmds[cursor..] are future (the 'undone' stack).
`do` slices off the future (O(n) allocation) — equivalent to `this.undone = []` in the two-stack version, just more expensive.
Two-stacks wins on do() cost (O(1) assignment vs O(n) slice) and is easier to reason about without index arithmetic.

options: Otherwise the next `redo` would re-apply both the new command and the stale undone commands as a batch
A fresh action creates a new branch; the previously-undone commands are no longer reachable
Without it, `cmd.apply()` would compose with the undone stack's pending reverts and cancel itself out
Clearing `undone` is what triggers the `done.push(cmd)` to fire — otherwise `do` is a no-op

questions.q: What pair of operations must each command expose?
options: execute / cancel — `cancel` aborts an in-flight command but cannot reverse a completed one
forward / backward — both run the same logic but with a direction flag passed in
commit / rollback — borrowed from transaction APIs, mapping `commit` to do and `rollback` to undo
Garbage-collected — once reverted, the command object has no remaining references
Moved from `done` to `undone` so redo can replay them
Stay in `done` but flagged with an `inverted: true` property; redo unsets the flag
Pushed to a third `redoQueue` that decouples reapplication from the original do/undo stacks

questions.q: What does `redo()` do when `undone` is empty?
options: Throws an `EmptyHistoryError` — the caller must check `canRedo()` before calling
Replays the last `done` command as a fallback, treating redo as a `repeat-last-action` shortcut
Returns `undefined` and silently re-applies the most recently undone command from a prior session

exercises.prompt: Complete History.do so that after do(+1), do(+2), undo, the value is 1.

L3.prompt: Build a History class with do/undo/redo over a number variable. Sequence: do(+1), do(+2), undo (now 1), do(+10) — clears redo. Then undo, undo. Log value after each step.
hints: Each command is `{ apply, revert }` — the History never inspects what they do.
do() must clear the undone stack — branching invalidates redo.
undo/redo are no-ops on empty stacks; return early instead of throwing.
